To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

In the manufacturing sectors of developing economies, there is no systematic evidence that the presence of inefficient firms, the existence of monopoly power in product or input markets, or the failure of firms to grow to an efficient size, is an important impediment to economic development.

(1) in most developing countries, manufacturing plants are relatively efficient; (2) the dispersion of firm-level productivity is low; (3) the degree of market power in product markets is low; and (4) there is little evidence of a lack of willingness to grow among small firms.
(1) manufacturing firms in developing countries perform relatively well, and (2) they do so because they are relatively efficient, not because they are protected or regulated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the performance and behavior of manufacturing firms in developing countries.
the following questions: (1) What is the role of manufacturing in the development process? (2) How do manufacturing firms in developing countries perform?
the performance of firms in developing countries and how this is influenced by market and non-market institutions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the manufacturing sectors in developing countries have many of the features that one would expect from a textbook model of a competitive economy.
the performance of the manufacturing sectors of developing economies is not systematically worse than that in industrial countries.
manufacturing sectors in developing countries are not doing very badly, but they have considerable scope to improve.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the manufacturing sectors of developing economies have much to offer, but also much to lose.
the manufacturing sectors of developing economies are surprisingly similar to those of industrial economies.
the manufacturing sectors of developing economies have many of the same features as those of developed economies, and the same issues of policy and regulation arise.
The main takeaway from our work is that

manufacturing firms in developing countries are surprisingly similar to those in developed countries in terms of performance and behavior, and that there are no obvious reasons to believe that they are less efficient or more subject to market failures than their counterparts in developed countries.
the conventional wisdom about manufacturing firms in developing countries is wrong.
manufacturing firms in developing countries are much less heterogeneous than commonly assumed, and that they are often surprisingly efficient.
